preview: Detailed interview experience at DE Shaw comprising an Online Assessment and three rigorous interview rounds covering DSA, OS, DBMS, LLD, HLD, and project discussions, culminating in a successful selection for the internship.
content: Who am I? Rushabh Mehta About this document It is my FULL interview experience written on the day of the interview and next day, thus I was able to recollect almost every question, details, and my answers. I have added links to resources of every concept used so if you are unfamiliar with any term you can simply click on it and learn about it. At the end I have added my own perspective, advice and preparation tips. Still if you have any doubts feel free to reach out to me. Eligibility Criteria CE, IT, Electrical, Electronics and EXTC students were eligible. CE, IT - 7 CPI and above Electrical, Electronics and EXTC - 8 CPI and above The Online Assessment (OA) Date: 5 July 2025 Duration: 60 minutes There were 3 DSA problems, every problem had a max time which you could spend on it I believe for the first problem 10 minutes and for the rest 2 problems 25 minutes each. You could switch between the problems freely. The OA was conducted on hackerrank, there was video proctoring, no tab switching allowed. There were options for almost all major languages like C/C++, Java, Python etc. Every problem was explained, had sample inputs and outputs, testcases, hidden testcases, constraints and input output format also. But we only had to complete a function like on LeetCode. According to me, the number of submissions and runs did not matter, only the number of test cases passed mattered. Here I have given problems as well as the solutions, feel free to try them on your own first before looking at the solutions. Problem 1: Very Easy You are given a string of n digits (0 to 9), and you have to repeatedly add adjacent digits and take the last digit of their sum and replace those 2 digits by it. We have to keep doing this until the string length is 2. Better explained by example: s = “4567” 4 5 6 7 9 1 3 // 4 + 5 = 09 so we take 9, 5 + 6 = 11 so we only take 1, 6 + 7 = 13 so we only take 3 0 4 // 9 + 1 = 10 so we only take 0, 1 + 3 = 4 Output: “04” Constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 2000 (I think) Solution: Brute forcing and just doing what the problem says is enough to pass all 10 test cases here. During OA in the first submission I actually forgot the edge case of n = 2 where we just return the string directly. I wasted 1 minute on this. I was able to solve this problem in 3 to 4 minutes. Problem 2: Hard to Very Hard (atleast for me) We are given a 0 indexed array of n integers named arr. In one move, you can select an index i in bounds of the array, and choose one of the 2 operations: 1. “Cover” all indices from max(0, i - arr[i] + 1) to i, inclusive 2. “Cover” all indices from i to min(n - 1, i + arr[i] - 1), inclusive You cannot choose an index ‘i’ more than 1 time. Return the minimum number of moves to “cover” the entire array. Examples: 1. arr = [2, 1], n = 2 Output: 1 Explanation: Here we can choose index 0 and apply the second operation. It will cover indices from [0, min(2 - 1, 0 + 2 - 1)] = [0, 1] … which is the whole array. 1. arr = [1, 2, 1, 1], n = 4 Output: 3 Explanation: We can choose index 1 and do first operation to cover indices [0, 1] Then choose any operation for index 2 to cover indices [2, 2] Then choose any operation for index 3 to cover indices [3, 3] Thus whole [0, 3] is covered in 3 operations. Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 500, 1 ≤ arr[i] ≤ n Solution: (Not done during OA) Apparently this can be solved by 1D DP or using a BFS like approach. I will describe the BFS approach briefly, basically you can build a graph of n + 1 nodes from 0 to n, and each possible [l, r) cover will be a directed edge from node l to node r. Each index has 2 possible covers we could choose from, so there will be 2 * (n + 1) directed edges. Since the cost of each operation is 1, we can do a BFS or Djikstra from node 0 to node n, and the distance of node n from node 0 will be the minimum number of moves. GPT Code is given below: def min_moves(arr): n = len(arr) # adjacency list for graph on vertices 0..n adj = [[] for _ in range(n+1)] for i, a in enumerate(arr): L = max(0, i - a + 1) R = min(n-1, i + a - 1) adj[L].append(i+1) # cover-left edge adj[i].append(R+1) # cover-right edge # BFS from 0 to find dist[n] dist = [float('inf')] * (n+1) dist[0] = 0 q = deque([0]) while q: u = q.popleft() for v in adj[u]: if dist[v] > dist[u] + 1: dist[v] = dist[u] + 1 q.append(v) return dist[n] In actual OA I did not figure out this solution at all, I did some stupid wrong solution and somehow I passed 5 / 15 test cases. Problem 3: Extremely Hard This was actually the exact problem: Codeforces Problem Link It is rated 2400 on Codeforces lol. Refer to its tutorial and comments under the tutorial blog post for the actual solution. It can be solved in multiple ways and involves monotonic stack, binary search etc. I did a very simple and approximate approach during the OA that incremented a counter when 2 consecutive elements are the same. I was able to pass only 9 / 15 test cases. As you can probably tell by now, OA problems can be crazy difficult, and they will, difficulty can vary drastically even in 1 year. But you have to keep your composure, and try to pass as many test cases as you can while being honest. Because that is what matters at the end. If you cheat in OA, you will be caught with the proctoring and you will not be shortlisted anyways … so there is no point. Maintain a good positive mindset and remain calm during the OA even if you can solve 0 problems fully, keep trying because it can help pass more test cases. 12 people including me were shortlisted after the OA. Date of Interview: 16 July 2025 Reporting Time: 8:30 AM I wore a formal white shirt and some pants and reached at around 8:10 or 8:15 AM, met with my friends and relaxed and talked. Round 1 I was the last one to be interviewed out of the 12. It was a virtual (online) interview on hackerrank code pair which is basically zoom meeting + shared codespace, around 1 hour duration. One interviewer (first) was already present, the other interviewer (second) got late by 5 to 10 minutes as he was having a login issue in hackerrank (too real). During this time when we were waiting for second to join, first and me started having some casual conversation about how our day had been so far, I told him I was excited for this interview, and that taking so many back to back interviews like this must be tiring for him, then we also talked about how I have also faced hackerrank login problem before … I admitted I was glad that the meet and the code pair link and everything was already set up for me. He also mentioned that he read my resume and asked me about my GSoC experience and how it was going. I told him that the acceptance rate this year was only 8% so I was happy I got accepted. After this second was able to join and the interview started. I gave my introduction which lasted for a minute, then interviewers also gave their intros. First had 12 years of experience and was an engineering manager named Uday and second had 4 years of experience and was named Pranav. We dived into the DSA portion of this interview. The second interviewer took the DSA portion. Problem 1: The question was pasted into the shared codespace and it was framed like this: There is a temperature sensor that gives reading of temperature outside everyday in celsius and we have been given the readings of the last n days. For every window of k consecutive days, we want to find the maximum temperature recorded in that window. Example: readings = [72, 69, 74, 73, 78, 65] and k = 3 Output: [74, 74, 78, 78] This problem is the same as Leetcode 239: Sliding Window Maximum. I first clarified the question by dry running manually on an example, then I asked if my manual output matched the expected output. Then I started talking about the brute force approach, that we can iterate through all windows of size k and for each window keep track of the maximum element and then put it in the output array. I mentioned time complexity was O(n * k) which is not optimal. I then went on to say that first window will look at indices [0, … k - 1] and second window [1, … k] that means every time we move a window by 1 place / go to the next window, only 1 new element is coming and only 1 old element is going, rest k - 2 elements are the same and thus we are doing this repeated work which we can try to eliminate. I then proceeded to tell them in a systematic manner that we need to maintain a monotonic invariant since we want to be getting the max of a window in O(1) time, we will keep some sort of container that has elements in this order. Then I explained this: (while simultaneously writing comments to explain working of the algo) [100, 20, 30] and k = 3 If we want to process these 3 elements, first we push 100 into the container, then comes 20, we push that as well. Now it is the turn of 30, notice that 30 > 20, thus there is no chance of 20 being the max for this window and for future windows too. Because there is not going to be any window which has 20 but not 30, thus we can just forget about this 20, and pop it from our container. So we will only store [100, 30]. And the max will be the leftmost element, which we can access in O(1) time. I also said that we will actually store the index of the elements instead of their value because we will also remove the elements which are “old” … i.e which are not in our current window anymore … for this we need the index. I then proceeded to talk about what data structure I would use for my “container”, I said that we are popping from both ends and inserting at the back, so we will need the deque data structure. The interviewer later asked me if there were any edge cases, I mentioned that if there was not even a single window of size k, implying that n < k then we can just return max of the array, and if an empty array is given as input then we can throw invalid argument error. After this they were satisfied and we moved onto the next problem, I was not asked to code my solution. Problem 2: There are n piles of stones, each pile of stones can have a different number of stones in it. Thus the array given was stones where stones[i] represent the number of stones in the i-th pile. We are also given integer k. In one “scoop” operation we can choose any contiguous window of size exactly k and scoop up all the stones in those k piles into a big pile placed at that same relative location. The number of stones in the big pile will be the sum of the stones in the individual “scooped up” k piles. We want to repeatedly perform this operation on the array until the array length is reduced to size 1, that is to say that only 1 element is left in the array. We also want to minimise our total effort in this process. Find that minimum effort. The effort associated with a single scoop operation is the total number of stones scooped up. Is it always possible to do this? I did not know this during the interview but this problem was another one directly from leetcode, and I had not seen or solved it: Leetcode 1000: Minimum Cost to Merge Stones. My solution here is not fully correct, don’t learn the solution, just read the experience part of it. I read the problem out loud step by step and understood every part of it except the part where it asked if it was not possible to do this, then we clarified that further and I finally told the interviewer that n % (k - 1) had to be 1 for the solution to exist. I explained the logic of modulo also by thinking out loud about repeated subtraction. (In one move the length of the array decreases by k - 1.) In hindsight I should also have mentioned that if k is 1 then it will give zero division error and it will be impossible to move stones from 1 pile to another as well. Then initially I thought of a Greedy strategy that out of every possible window we can always choose the one with the minimum sum, the interviewer asked me that will it always lead to the optimal solution? Then I got the hint that maybe it was a DP problem, so I explained that maybe not taking the minimum at current state can benefit future states … so we have to systematically explore the state space of the problem and dynamic programming was a way to achieve this. Then I said that for every single index (valid index where the window can start) we have 2 choices: Either scoop this window and go to the next state, or don’t scoop it and move to the next index. We will return the minimum of these two possibilities. It was somewhat conceptually clear but the implementation of it, more specifically what to track in dp state was not clear at all to me. Since we cannot modify the array every time obviously because it would be too slow. I basically got stuck here … the interviewer gave the same hint repeatedly that we do not need to change the array and actually compute the “new” element after a scoop operation, but I did not understand him. He also asked me at one point how we will find the sum of k consecutive elements quickly? I answered that we can maintain a Prefix Sum array where the i-th element will store the sum of 0 … i indices and how to get sum of l … r from that as well, I actually should have mentioned this sooner … It was obvious to me so I skipped it, but that is not a good practice in an interview. What may be obvious to you still needs to be communicated to the interviewer. I ultimately ended up saying that we will need to track whether this index is real or already removed using a n bit integer mask (Bitmasking), I believe this is possible but not very implementation friendly either. After this he said that in the interest of time we will move to the next portion of the interview … I was more than happy to lol. No actual code implementation again. Now the first interviewer started talking. This was the CSF (Computer Science Fundamentals) part of the interview. Questions asked on OS: “You built a multi-threaded application in which there are some shared open files, an RDBMS with many rows, and it works fine for the most part, but sometimes it completely freezes. Why do you think this happens?” First I explained that since we have multiple threads accessing shared resources like open files and accessing the same database rows. For this purpose we would have implemented some sort of locking mechanism so that when a thread wants to write to a shared resource, no other thread can access it. This can create dependencies and those dependencies can be circular in nature … cycle in dependency graph, leading to a Deadlock. So the application will completely freeze in this case. In this part I accidentally said the word “transaction” instead of “thread” many times, and later corrected myself … do be careful in interviews about this. Then he asked me what sort of solution do we have for this deadlock problem? I explained that since deadlocks CAN in fact happen, we would need to handle them somehow. I said that we can use Banker’s Algorithm which uses data like how many shared resources are available, how many are needed by processes, how many resources are remaining etc to detect whether it should allocate this resource or not. Then he said that this is correct but we want another more suitable solution and that “think from an application point of view”. So I suggested something along these lines: We prevent deadlocks from ever happening by making sure that whenever a thread requests a resource, and some other thread is using it, we don’t let it wait, instead we just delay it to sometime later, or we can kill that thread. He was satisfied with this answer. See Deadlock Prevention for more in depth understanding. Then we also talked about “what can go wrong” when multiple threads access shared data. We had a discussion about Race Conditions and I explained it by example of a simple shared integer x being incremented by 2 threads. He was satisfied with this, then he asked me how to not let them access the same shared data. I started explaining about Semaphores and how they work, how they prevent shared data access, mutual exclusion etc concepts. We did not go super in depth into this. Questions on DBMS: “Now your web application is working very slow most of the time, and you have debugged and found out that the database queries are taking a lot of time, so how would you optimize these queries? Assume the database is an RDBMS.” First I said that we should ensure we are using correct and optimal SQL keywords in our query, like for example if we want to display top 3 users, and our query just selects all users from database, and only in our application backend logic we are sorting … then it is highly inefficient since the database engine is developed for such kind of work only. Also in SQL we should use the LIMIT keyword like after an ORDER BY and then LIMIT 3 for top 3 values. Then he said okay but even this is not fast enough for our application, what more can we do? I said we can create an Index on the columns which are accessed frequently in our queries. They will help us reduce the number of disk block retrievals. Then he said I want you to dive deeper into the working of the index. So I thought of table (user_id, age) and we want to filter 18+ users, so we can create an index on the age column, so now the query which would have taken a full table scan would only take an index scan. I also said that a smart implementation would also store index values in sorted order so we can answer queries using divide and conquer binary search instead of a naive linear search. Then he asked me if there is any disadvantage to creating an index, if there was nothing we would just create an index on every column right… I said this dialogue “This is computer science, there is always a trade off.” And then explained that whenever we insert or update a row, the corresponding indices will also have to be updated, that will have some additional overhead, also the index will contain column value and pointers (disk addresses) to the corresponding disk blocks, this will use additional memory … There are also 2 types of indexes: sparse and dense and if we create a dense index then there will be an index entry for every row in the database. This was it for the technical part of the interview, they asked me If I wanted to ask them something, I asked the following question: “Recently a month ago around 16-17th June there was a massive google cloud outage for 6 to 8 hours (more in the us east and central regions, many organisations who had services dependent on it (like Discord) also went down, if something outage like this were to happen again but affect India more, and specifically DE Shaw’s work, how would the firm handle this?” and they answered it discussing cloud SLA and various strategies like backups and other safety measures etc. Always ask something interesting at the end of the interview if they give you the chance. 5 people including me made it to round 2. Round 2 Again I was last to be giving this interview, it was offline and on pen and paper. The duration was around 1 hour + some 10 minutes. There were again 2 male interviewers, both seemed to be very senior and mature and thus they had a more serious look in the interview compared to the last one. First they asked me about how my OA was and was I able to solve all 3 of the questions? I said no and explained how my OA went. I told them that in the second problem I did sort of a greedy approach which was only able to pass partial TCs, and later when I re-attempted it, put it into an AI tool, I realised that it was a DP problem. Then they asked me what was the difference between a greedy approach and a DP approach. I explained that a greedy solution just takes a look at all possible next states, and just chooses a locally optimal one blindly, without thinking that “okay maybe if I skip taking the immediate best thing, maybe it leads to an even better solution overall”. Compared to that, dynamic programming is a way to systematically explore all possible states of the problem space and choose the actual globally best solution. Then he asked me, “Do you think every greedy problem can be solved using DP?” I said that in a greedy problem, making a sequence of locally optimal choices leads to a globally optimal solution, so in the case of DP even if we explore more states we will still reach that optimal solution, so yes every greedy problem is a DP problem. Then he gave me a piece of paper which had some very roughly written C code written on it like this: #include <stdio.h> char *get_string() { char* s[100]; s = "Hello World\0"; return s; } char *get_string2() { char *s = malloc(100); s <- "Hello World\0" // comment by me: think of this as strcpy(s, "Hello ..") return s; } int main() { char *s1 = get_string(); char *s2 = get_string2(); print(s1); // what will this print ? free(s2); print(s2); // what will this print ? return 0; } Keep in mind that the syntax might be all off. I was really confused by this problem since even though C was my first language, it had been a long time since I used it. I said some things that maybe print s1 will print the actual hello world and s2 will print the pointer like <0xAB392…> logical address. Then I straight up said that I was not very familiar with languages where string was not a native datatype. Then he asked me if I knew about the concept of “Dangling Pointers”. I said that I had heard of the term but was not familiar, and I think it had to do something with memory safety and memory leaks. He said it was not related to that and we moved on. Next problem I was given was: You have to design a Priority-Based Task Scheduler where: 1. Each task has a unique integer ID. 2. Each task has a priority from 0 to 9, higher priority means we would like to finish that task earlier. 3. Tasks can have dependencies like A -> B means that task A cannot be scheduled until and unless task B has finished. There is no constraint on the number of dependencies or their nature. 4. We have to implement this interface: 1. add(task_id, priority, dependencies) -> adds the task to our scheduler 2. cancel(task_id) -> removes this task from our scheduler 3. get_next_ready_task() -> returns the highest priority task who does not have any pending dependencies He asked me how I would model and store this data, what data structures and algorithms I would use and how I would implement this system as a whole. It clearly was a mix of an (Low Level Design) LLD-ish problem along with DSA. I would say that my solutions and explanations were correct here but not as good as I would like, maybe the interviewer was NOT satisfied here? Who knows. First I clarified that there could be a cycle in the dependencies of the task, so this was it for the edge cases part. Then he again asked how would I model and store the data … so I responded that we have 2 entities here, the task which I could model as a Task class, and the Scheduler class which would implement the actual interface and act as the orchestrator class. Then I drew an example (no cycle) and showed that we need to Topologically Sort this dependency graph and out of all the nodes who did not have any pending dependencies, we can return the highest priority one … for this we can modify the BFS-like approach of Kahn’s algorithm, which uses a FIFO Queue and instead use a Max Heap there, where the “key” of the max heap will be the priority of the task object, so we can extract the max from the heap in O(1) time. Then he counter questioned that will you topo sort the graph every time get_next..() is called? I said no since that would be wasteful, instead we will compute the topo sort once and then store it. Then he again asked what would happen when you add or cancel a task then? I said for cancelling a task, I would just store it in a Hash Set, and check that the output of get_next..() is not in the cancelled set in O(1) time, also whenever a task is cancelled, all of the tasks which are dependent on it (not the dependencies of the task) would also need to be cancelled recursively in a DFS-like fashion. So for this I would need to store a list of dependents as well as dependencies in the Task object. Again he said that what if you want to remove a cancelled task from the dependents list? That will require a lot of array operations. So I said that again we can use a hash set for those 2 lists as well to support deletion in O(1) time. Also since we are given task_id as an argument in the cancel() method, we need to also have a Hash Map which maps each unique task_id to its corresponding Task object. In the middle of all this discussion he was sort of tired at one point and said that you need to write all the data structures we are using in 1 place. I do not think he was happy with my “figure it out as you go approach” of solving this problem. He also wanted me to write pseudocode for the cancel() method during which I mentioned the map and stuff, so it was kind of all over the place. This was the most not-good part of the whole interview experience. At one point in the discussion I even mentioned the Observer Pattern for signalling that a task has been deleted to all of its dependents. My solution was hella complicated and I surely missed something simpler. He said in the interest of time we will move forward to the next portion of the interview. Now the other interviewer started talking. He asked me if I knew what Virtual Memory was. I answered in a systematic manner that disk storage is large and cheaply available, but it takes a lot of time to access stored data from disk, for this reason we have a much faster but smaller in size memory called Main Memory or RAM. In main memory we can randomly access any portion of it in constant time. I then explained that since it is in smaller size, we would like to have a larger Main Memory, virtual memory is exactly the solution to this problem. Then I started explaining Paging by myself only, I did not want him to dive into Segmentation as I had not really studied that in depth. So I explained the Page Table and its working and how it allows us to have more number of so-called virtual addresses than there are actual addresses in main memory. Then he asked if I knew what a Frame was, I said I am not aware, it was an easy question I should have known. Then he asked what happens when the page table gets completely filled up. I said since we cannot increase the size of the main memory, we will have to replace a page in the table. For this purpose we can use an FCFS replacement approach which just works like FIFO, the older pages are moved back onto disk. Then he asked if there were better approaches, I said we could use an LRU replacement policy which always replaces the page who has been accessed the least recently i.e most oldest accessed page. Then he actually straight up asked me how I would implement this LRU replacement style page table. This is similar to Leetcode 146: LRU Cache. I explained that since we want to remove the “oldest” accessed page quickly, we would need to maintain some sort of monotonic invariant, and even pages which are accessed after LRU page and before MRU page need to be able to move to the MRU position quickly. For this reason I suggested we store references of the pages in a Doubly Linked List. Then I said that to find an arbitrary page, we would again need to scan through the whole DLL, that would be linear in time with respect to size of the page table. Instead of this we can maintain a hash map that stores page_id as key and reference to the linked list node as the value. So we can directly jump to that particular node in O(1) time, do a finite number of pointer manipulations and maintain the DLL invariant. Thus all operations are O(1) time here. DLL will look like: [LRU page < - > page < - > … < - > MRU page] (here, < - > denotes both forward and backward links) He was satisfied with this. Then he asked me if I was familiar with vectors (std::vector in C++) I said yes a vector is just a dynamic array. So he said that I want you to show me how it is implemented using a static array. I first said that we will declare a static array of some fixed size n, then keep an integer pointer index which will point to the next index where we can write the next element. Then I explained inserting an element and removing an element from the end in O(1) time, and in the middle of the array in O(n) time due to the fact that we have to move the rest of the elements. Then we got to the main case where the array has to dynamically expand in insertion. I said that we will go from an n size array to a 2n size static array. And I explained that we will only have to do this expensive operation (from both memory and time perspective) 1 time. He said why exactly do we double? I said that we get O(1) amortized insertion complexity at the end of the array due to it. He asked me to explain how. Say we insert 2n = O(n) elements, it will take us n * O(1) + O(n) * O(1) + (n - 1) * O(1) = O(n) total time. Explanation: first n elements will take constant time to insert, then the boundary element takes O(n) time as we allocate new n size memory, rest n - 1 elements again take constant time. Thus O(n) elements took O(n) total time, thus a single element took O(n) / O(n) = O(1) amortized time. This is how you do amortized analysis of an algorithm, and it's also exactly what satisfied him. I also went on to explain that if we increase size by some constant amount like 5 new slots, insertion at the end would be O(n) amortized instead. He again counter questioned that what if we take 2 raised to n. I said that if n was even as small as 100, we would have to allocate 2 raised to 100 memory, which is a lot and would probably go to waste. Then he said that you said that we can access any array element in constant time, so how is that implemented or possible. I explained that in C/C++ lets say we declare an array arr like this int arr[100]; // declares a static integer array of size 100 The arr variable actually is a pointer to the 0-th index in the contiguous memory block. Let us say we want to access 5th element arr[5], actually what happens is arr + 5 is computed … this is called Pointer Arithmetic and then this (memory location) pointer is then de-referenced to get the actual value at that spot. arr[5] is actually *(arr + 5) in C/C++. Then he asked, "Let's say I declare a char array which starts from memory location x (like arr = x), and in a separate context I declare an integer array which starts from memory location x as well. So will the exact memory location of the 5-th element be the same in both arrays?” First I did not understand how 2 arrays could start at the same exact location, then he again said they were in separate contexts, so I thought he meant like both arrays were part of different processes and those processes have their own independent address spaces, so it's not possible that the actual physical address of both is same. But then he again said that they were in the same address space, but not like this. Then I guess it struck me on its own that he wanted the difference due to the types, so I said that the size to store 1 int is 4 bytes on most systems and a char is just 1 byte. So both the 5-th elements could not be at exactly the same byte due to size difference. Then he asked how is this accounted for in *(arr + 5) so I explained that it would actually be: *(arr + 5 * sizeof(int)). Then he asked what about user defined data types like Structs? I said in this case the size of the struct can be computed as the sum of the sizes of its members. Then he wrote this struct definition on paper: struct S { int a; char b; float *c; } and asked me how much would be the size of this struct? I immediately recalled Type Alignment in Structs (I had seen many LinkedIn posts talking about it), I did not know in depth but enough to answer something. I said that again int was 4 bytes, the char was only 1 byte but there is a minimum sort of size that we can allocate, for example we can't just allocate 3 bits or something. So there would be again 3 extra bytes of padding associated with this char, if say the min size was 4 bytes. And for the pointer the type did not matter as all pointers occupy the same amount of space as just an address … an integer at the end. It could be 8 bytes, let's say then the size of struct would be 4 + 4 + 8 = 16 bytes. They were fine with this answer, but again they asked how can we find the actual size of the pointer variable? I said if main memory was of n bytes then we would need around floor(log2(n)) + 1 (actual formula is ceiling of log2(n)) bits to represent every address in it, thus pointer would be of that many bits … and we can convert to bytes too by dividing by 8. Then he said that take example for n = 2 raised to 32. In this case we only needed 32 bits so therefore 4 bytes for a pointer variable. Then he asked me if I knew the difference between a 32 bit and 64 bit system. I said that the difference was that we need 32 bits to represent an address in a 32 bit system and similarly for 64 bits. I don't know if this is correct or not. Then he looked at my resume which was kept on the table and he asked me can you explain the work that you have done for SymPy in GSoC? I proceeded to first explain them what SymPy actually does: I explained the difference between numerical computation libraries and a symbolic one like SymPy. I talked about the fact that numerical libraries are optimized for crunching numbers, plotting etc. But SymPy solves everything mathematically and allows us to get a formula where we can analyse term by term the significance of every one of our input variables and how they affect our dependent quantity. I explained this again with an example that say f(x) = x ** 2, then we know that derivative would be f dash(x) = 2 * x, a numerical library would only be able to compute this derivative at a point like x = 5, but SymPy can compute it just in symbolic terms. Side Note: My interviewer did not understand and asked me if x ** 2 and 2 * x were same or what I was saying, I again said 2 * x was derivative, then I used the word “differentiation” then he remembered his old days I guess and understood. Being a math oriented person, I thought it was very funny. Then they asked me about my exact project. I explained that SymPy has a physics module as well which allows us to simulate any physics - physical situation with forces, torques etc in terms of its objects and classes, and then we can get the equations of motion simply by calling a method. I drew a pulley and 2 blocks as an example and said that we can model this situation and get acceleration of the blocks directly. Then I said in these types of situations we can make use of geometry of the situation like radius of circular pulley for the torque. So my work was to develop these geometry objects and integrate them in the bigger physics module. Then they asked me some HR type question “What was the biggest challenge you faced in this project?”. I cooked the following story (85 % true): When I got accepted into GSoC they immediately informed me that the developer who had actually started with creation of this module had left his work incomplete 2 years ago and left the open source community. Also there was not much documentation to help me. I think this answered their question but I continued to say that I singlehandedly did this task and figured out the intended use case of the code without any examples or docs. After that I developed comprehensive docs and usage examples for the module, and also I was working on another geometry object which would model the cone. He also asked how many lines of code I had written approximately since joining, I said around 1000-1200 lines of code. I had mentioned (and bolded) in my resume that I worked on developing unit tests as well for SymPy, so he asked what was the average test coverage percentage of my module, I answered 80 to 85 percent (had no idea of actual number). They asked if I already knew python getting accepted into the GSoC program, I said I knew python for 2 years and was also contributing as a normal open source contributor as well. They also asked what technologies I learnt while working, I said I learnt Python better, learnt Sphinx for documentation and became familiar with GitHub Actions for CI/CD. I think this was it and then they gave me the opportunity to ask them anything I wanted. I asked the following question: “Regardless if an intern secures PPO or not, what does success look like for an intern in this role?” Both of them answered covering different aspects of the internship like networking, proactiveness and that was it for round 2. All 5 of us were in another room waiting for the results to be announced. After like 10 minutes of waiting I was again called for a much shorter Round 3 !. This was only to re-evaluate me I guess, round 3 did not happen for any of the other candidates. I was like wtf sure let’s do it. I went for it. Round 3 Shorter interview around 25-30 minutes, technically again I was the last person to be giving this one (as I was the only one lol). There was 1 male and 1 female interviewer. They both asked me 1 problem each. No introductions, direct problems. Problem 1: It was explained verbally by the male interviewer. You are given an array of stock prices and you can do at most 2 transactions, and you cannot have more than 1 purchased stock at a time. We want the maximum possible profit. I clarified that whether the limit of 2 was fixed or it can be an input parameter like K, it was fixed to be 2 only. This is the same as Leetcode 123: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock 3. I explained that we can make either 0, or 1 or 2 transactions. So for every single stock, if we have not already completed our 2 transactions, we have some amount of choices. After hearing this he directly told me to tell the transition, which I did in the following way while writing the pseudocode on paper. If we are currently holding a stock, you may choose to sell it at current price, or you may choose to keep holding it. And if we are not currently holding a stock, we may choose to buy the stock at current price, or skip it. Thus we only needed to maintain the current index, whether I am holding a stock or not, and how many transactions have I completed. Using this we can build a recursive dynamic programming solution. [There also exists a greedy solution by tracking some min and max values … but since he said the word transition I got fixed on DP.] He was satisfied with my solution. Problem 2: Given by the female interviewer. There is a game which around 10 million daily active users play, each user has a score associated with them based on how well they play the game. We have to design a leaderboard which shows the top 10 players along with their scores in real time. Actually this problem was somewhat similar to: Leetcode 1244: Design a Leaderboard, I had solved it before but I came up with a different solution in the interview. Actually during the interview I felt that this problem was phrased in such a way that it sounded like a High Level Design (HLD) problem, so I clarified on from what angle we wanted to approach this, “do we want object design (referring to LLD) or something else?” She said “not object design no” and then I again asked if these 10 million users were actually concurrent users, so she said yes they are concurrent and this number 10 million is only given so that I understand the scale at hand then I thought okay we will see how to implement this in HLD. I started talking about how we will have 2 application services - one server handling the game logic, and another for the Leaderboard, etc. She said leave the architecture aside and tell me how we will get the top 10. This was my thought process: We will obviously have stored these user id and their scores in some sort of database be it relational or not, but reading from db and updating takes lot of time, so we will actually write the updates to score that happen to an in-memory database (like redis or memcached), she actually counter questioned that will data of 10 million users fit into single instance? I said no we can actually distribute users into 2 or more instances. She said let's take 10 such instances so that each one handles only 1 million users. In my mind I was like, "great this does seem like an HLD problem only”. Then I talked about how from each instance we can get top 10 … it will be easier than getting from 10 million users directly, and we can merge the 10 * 10 = 100 users data again taking top 10 from them. [Side Note: She did not let me finish my entire design … so I thought to add it here in case anyone is prepping HLD as well. After getting the top 10 from these 100 users … returned by all 10 instances, we can update the leaderboard very quickly … and then to maintain the database updated we will periodically flush the data from these in-memory db instances to the actual db. High level overview of my system (I have only shown 3 instances, it should be 10): She was like let us not think about query performance and everything, just tell me logic wise what would you do to get the top 10 users ?, just assume that the scores are given in an array. I realised they wanted to ask another DSA problem only, I would have realised sooner if she did not say that they were concurrent users, I do not think concurrent updates we can get in an array like this. So I said that we can process all 10 million users and maintain a min heap of size 10 and explained by example that if 1, 2, … 10 were in min heap, we would check the top of min heap (1) in O(1) time against the score we are currently processing (say 11) and if 11 > 1 we will pop from min heap and insert 11. She was finally happy with the min heap approach. Then later she asked how will you handle an update of a user’s score who is on the leaderboard? I said that we can use bubble up and bubble down operations in the heap implementation, this will handle updates in the heap in O(log(10)) time. Then she asked me to write TC and explain all 4 operations: add a new user, update a user’s score, delete a user, get the leaderboard. Also they had asked how will you handle when a player who is not on the leaderboard gets a better score than some of the top 10 players? I said in this case we will have to maintain a max heap of the remaining players, and whenever an update happens, we will check the max of max heap and compare it to the min of the min heap, if the max is greater, we will pop from both heaps and exchange the elements. For deletion again we can simply remove the user and maintain the heap invariant using bubble up / down operations in O(log 10) or O(log n), depending on which heap the user is in. Getting the leaderboard is just reading the values of min heap and then reversing them. Thus we can use 2 heaps in this way to solve this problem. They again asked, is there anything else that you can think about that we can support here? I said that could depend on the domain of the game. They said not in that sense, just solution wise. After a pause for 5 seconds I said I could not think of anything and that “this looks like a good leaderboard”, the interviewer laughed and that was it. Round 3 over. After some more minutes of waiting the results were announced, 2 people were selected, one of them was me!. It was 2 / 5 = 0.40 probability and I did it. Final Thoughts and Advice + Resources I really liked DE Shaw’s interview process. The interviewers do ask questions in depth as you saw but they also do guide you in the direction of the correct approach if you are thinking out loud. All in all they tested DSA, CSF (OS, DBMS, OOP), C/C++ Language Specifics, LLD, HLD, Resume/Projects, and HR questions. Here are all the resources I prepared from and my advice in general and about how to approach the questions in an interview: 1. DSA and CP: Striver’s A to Z DSA Sheet Neetcode 150 Roadmap Both of the above resources group the problems by their patterns and topics, which is absolutely crucial for mastering DSA. Start with them, do not attempt any random problems in the start of your DSA journey, learn to think systematically and in terms of patterns. CP 31 Sheet by TLE Eliminators for more ad-hoc and logical thinking. LeetCode POTD, LeetCode and Codeforces contests should be attempted, they are not pattern-wise and will help you explore newer and more niche topics as well. After attempting a contest, always analyse and upsolve the problems you could not do in a contest. While attempting any DSA problem in an interview, first read and understand the problem, clarify it with example input and output if necessary, talk through any possible edge cases, input constraints, assumptions you have made etc. The initial question given to you by the interviewer may be vague on purpose to see if you can clarify and understand problem requirements. Then start with a basic-naive-brute-force approach, and continually improve it by pointing out its flaws (like repeated work) and getting to the more optimal solution. THINK OUT LOUD and explain everything to your interviewer in a systematic manner. Do mention time and space complexity trade offs. Learn how to find time and space complexity of any algorithm (or data structure operation) (both normal and amortized) beyond just counting the number of loops. This is the most practice heavy subject that is tested and you should have already started preparing this earlier, you cannot prepare this subject enough. Jitna karo utna kam hain. 2. CSF: 1. Object Oriented Programming: GFG top OOP questions InterviewBit top OOP questions Coder Army LLD playlist first few videos (they cover OOP + SOLID in depth) You should cover this from the perspective of either C++ or Java. I went with C++ here as I was already familiar with the language, but Java provides a more “complete” view of OOP for example it has interfaces while in C++ we have to use abstract classes for it. Key topics to cover: ○ Classes, Objects, Constructor etc basic terms ○ Inheritance, Polymorphism, Encapsulation, Abstraction - the 4 pillars ○ The diamond problem and its solution (the virtual keyword in C++) ○ SOLID principles This is a very foundational topic that you must cover in as much depth as you can. You will need this as a foundation when you study software engineering and Low Level System Design. 2. Operating Systems: Love Babbar OS Roadmap Striver Core OS Sheet Bedtime Stories on Operating Systems (short book quick for revision) Reference Books like Tanenbaum / Galvin Key topics: ○ Processes, Threads (their differences, PCB, context switching etc) ○ CPU Scheduling Algorithms (Round Robin, FIFO etc) ○ Concurrency problems (Deadlocks, Race Conditions) and their solutions - Semaphores, Locks etc ○ Memory Management techniques - Paging and Segmentation ■ Page Replacement Algorithms ■ Fragmentation ■ Memory allocation techniques ○ In general understanding of CPU, RAM and the disk and how they interact Extra infrequent topics but good to know: ○ File System ○ Disk Scheduling Algorithms ○ Bootup process 3. Database Management Systems: College course textbooks DBMS Roadmap by Love Babbar DBMS Sheet by Striver Website to practice writing SQL queries SQL Questions on leetcode Key topics: ○ Data, types of DBMS - (RDBMS, Key Value stores, document databases, graph databases etc) and their tradeoffs ○ RDBMS - how they store data, tables, relations ○ ACID guarantees, their meaning ○ Two phase locking (I didnt do other algos lol) ○ Isolation Levels ○ Indexing, its tradeoffs, types of indices, what fields should you index ○ SQL practice - JOINs, Subqueries, execution order 4. Computer Networks: I didn’t prepare this as CE had it in sem 5, not sem 4 like IT did. DE Shaw had asked TPO for courses done by the branches till now and seeing that CE did not have CN, I was not asked anything related to it. If you do have this subject, prepare it thoroughly. 5. Low Level Design Coder Army LLD playlist This subject has OOP and SOLID principles as pre-reqs. Just learn the general flow of how to approach an object design problem in an interview. Do 4 or 5 practice problems and you are done. Optionally you can cover a few famous design patterns, I covered the following - Singleton, Observer, Adapter, Factory, Strategy. 6. High Level Design NeetCode system design videos, discussions etc System Design Primer on GitHub This is not required as such for preparation I think, but somehow it made its way into my interview. I had studied it though. 7. Resume / Projects / HR questions Make a well formatted resume, have solid projects in domains you have explored - web, app, ai ml etc. For every project you must know what you did in it, what challenges you faced, why you made it, impact of the project and what would you do differently if you had to rebuild it. Prepare standard HR questions, learn to give little fake HR answers as well (make up scenarios) 8. C/C++ (or any) language specifics There are many debugging questions, in general questions like top 50 C++ interview questions etc on GFG, interviewbit and the like, do them properly. Also have a general curiosity of “how is it working internally” whenever you use something in your language. Thank you for reading this. I hope it was helpful. Feel free to reach out to me. All the best!
